gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the same-size nameplates deliver very different energy: the Pecron F5000LFP's 7,200 W is a 240 V figure (3,600 W at 120 V), and The Solar Lab measured it at 84% efficiency with about 52 W idle draw, so its 5,120 Wh works out to about 4,300 Wh against the 4.87 kWh Andrew Riha got from the 5,024 Wh Anker SOLIX S5000 (about 10 W idle).
standout_why: Compared against the pages I could open: OffGrid Current's whole-home page (cited), powerstations.reviews (cited), The Solar Lab's big-stations roundup (cited), and Jackery's product page (429, not read). Popular Mechanics and Car and Driver (both cited) could not be fetched, so I know them only through ChatGPT's answer. OffGrid Current already lists cycle life with thresholds (Jackery 4,000 to 70%, Anker 6,000 to 80%) and idle draw (Jackery 50 W, Anker 8.8 W) but never puts them on one basis, has no Pecron row and no measured capacity, and says it has not tested the units. Popular Mechanics, per ChatGPT's answer, has the Anker's ~4,900 Wh delivered and low standby, so the Anker half of the finding is already out there. powerstations.reviews shows the Pecron at 5,120 Wh / 7,200 W with surge 'not published' and no 120 V limit, efficiency or idle figure in the part I could read (the last 17k characters of its table were not read). The Solar Lab roundup does not mention the Pecron at all; the 84% / 52 W / 3,600 W-at-120 V figures are on its separate Pecron review, which was not among ChatGPT's results. ChatGPT applied a flat 15% loss to every unit and called the Pecron a '7,200 W value contender' with no caveat.
decides: It confirms the Anker SOLIX S5000 over the Pecron F5000LFP for the question's core use (a day or two of 120 V essentials), not on headline specs but on delivered energy and idle drain. With the inverter on and no load, the Pecron's measured 52 W burns about 24% of its nameplate per day; the Anker's measured ~10 W burns about 5%. It also narrows the Jackery/Pecron/TITAN '7,200 W' advantage to 240 V loads: the one unit I could source a 120 V limit for (Pecron) gives 3,600 W there, less than the 120 V-only TITAN 5000 Classic's 4,000 W and no more than a 30 A RV outlet carries. It does not overturn the Jackery or a 7,200 W unit as the pick for 240 V well pumps or central AC. Caveats: the Anker figure is app-reported rather than metered (Riha), the Pecron figure is an efficiency percentage from a different lab, and the Anker's 15-16 week ship time in the research notes still governs whether it can be the pick. I could not read any maker-store price or ship notice today.

findings.label: Delivered energy on a full discharge (named reviewer)
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review: 5 kWh on wheels, tested through a real power outage (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha, 2026-10-28)
findings.note: Riha: 'the app reported 4.87 kWh delivered on a full discharge, 97% of nameplate'. App-reported, not externally metered; discharge used the 120 V outlets only. He also quotes Anker's rated discharge efficiency: 96% at 1,000 W, 90.5% at 4,500 W.

findings.label: Idle draw, 120 V output on, nothing connected (measured vs stated)
findings.value: about 10 W measured (5% of charge lost in 24 h); 8.8 W stated by Anker
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha)
findings.note: Arithmetic: 10 W × 24 h = 240 Wh/day = 4.8% of 5,024 Wh. Riha also quotes Anker's standby rating of 21 days (512 h) at 120 V and 14 days (341 h) at 240 V. The 8.8 W figure is also on Anker's page https://www.ankersolix.com/s5000 (read 2026-11-27).

findings.label: Round trip and 120 V wall charging (measured)
findings.value: 6.24 kWh from the wall for a full charge at the 1,800 W setting, a 78% round trip; 1.79 kW for 2 h 49 min, then about 1.43 kW for the last 50 min
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha)
findings.note: Total is about 3 h 39 min at 120 V. Anker's own footnote: at 120 V the 1,800 W rate is limited to under three hours when current exceeds 12 A. 240 V charging was not tested by Riha.

findings.label: Fridge runtime in a real outage (measured)
findings.value: 61.5 hours from 100% to 18%, about 65 W average; Riha estimates 75 hours on a full charge
findings.source_title: Anker Solix S5000 deep-dive review (pv magazine USA, Andrew Riha)
findings.note: PSPS outage test on Riha's own refrigerator. Anker's claim is up to 86 hours for a 700 L fridge at 25 °C.

findings.label: Maker's specs: output, cycle life, charging, solar, UPS, weight
findings.value: 4,500 W continuous, 8,000 W peak (no duration given); 10,000 cycles to more than 60% capacity; AC input 1,800 W max at 120 V, 4,500 W max at 240 V; solar 1,000 W (11-60 V, 17 A) + 2,000 W (16-165 V, 17 A); UPS ≤10 ms; 97 lb net; 5-year warranty; UL 9540 and UL 9540A
findings.note: The product page headlines cycle life at the 60% threshold. The fetched text carried no price, no ship notice and no per-outlet watt ratings.

findings.label: Cycle life at the 80% threshold (maker)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX S5000 specs (Anker SOLIX blog)
findings.note: Same page: recharge about 99 min at 240 V, about 3.1 h at 120 V, about 2.1 h with both solar inputs. Normalising to Jackery's 70% threshold: a straight line between Anker's two points gives roughly 8,000 cycles at 70%, about twice Jackery's 4,000. That interpolation is my arithmetic, not an Anker figure. 6,000 daily cycles = 16.4 years.

findings.label: AC output at 120 V vs 240 V
findings.source_title: Pecron F5000LFP Review: The Best Cheap Power Station for Home Backup? (The Solar Lab)
findings.note: The Solar Lab: '3,600W at 120V, or 7,200W at 240V'. Pecron publishes no surge rating; The Solar Lab says it ran 'well above' the rated output but gives no number.

findings.label: Measured efficiency and idle draw (named reviewer)
findings.value: 84% efficiency; about 52 W with the inverter on and nothing connected
findings.note: Arithmetic: 5,120 Wh × 0.84 = about 4,300 Wh delivered, about 570 Wh less than the Anker's 4.87 kWh despite a nameplate 96 Wh larger. 52 W × 24 h = 1,248 Wh/day = 24% of nameplate; 5,120 / 52 = about 98 h to empty at idle alone, against Anker's rated 512 h standby at 120 V. The review gives no measured Wh, no author name and no date beyond a 2026 copyright.

findings.label: Charging, solar input, weight (named reviewer)
findings.value: No 240 V charging input; 30 A port takes up to 3,600 W, 1 h 40 min empty to full (measured); standard 120 V outlet about 3.5 h (measured); solar 6,400 W (2 × 3,200 W); 124 lb
findings.note: The Solar Lab: 'it cannot accept a 240V charging input'. UPS is supported on the 120 V plugs; no switchover time given. Price at review was $1,899 with the reviewer's code; not a price for today.

findings.label: Cycle life, surge and standby as a rival page states them (not the maker)
findings.value: 4,000 cycles to 70%; 7,200 W continuous, 14,400 W surge; 50 W standby; 134.5 lb; 120/240 V
findings.note: Secondary source; OffGrid Current says it has not tested the units, and I could not check these against Jackery (see unsourced). Arithmetic if the 50 W holds: 50 W × 24 h = 1,200 Wh/day = 24% of 5,040 Wh. The same page gives the Anker as 6,000 cycles to 80% and 8.8 W idle but never reconciles the thresholds.
